message: How can this act fail, beyond what its contexts already say? Name each failure, or say deed:Nothing. An unnamed failure reaches the actor as text they must parse.
Say in one sentence what this act does, in words an actor would use. If the sentence needs 'and', consider two acts.
What does the actor get back when this act succeeds? Exactly one outcome: a single value or a stream. 'It prints some lines' is not an answer: what would a program do with it?
What does the actor supply? List the parameters in order, or say deed:Nothing. An act with no input is fine; an act that has not said so is undecided.

What does the environment supply? A target the act runs against, a credential, a policy: name each context, or say deed:Nothing. If the actor must repeat a value on every act of a session, it is context, not input.

What existing state does this act read? Name each state, or say deed:Nothing. Whoever may perform the act will be allowed to read exactly this, so an act that reads more than it says is a leak and one that says more than it reads is over-privileged.
What is the value the actor gets back, or each value of the stream? Name its kind. If it has no name, nobody downstream can depend on it.

What state does this act write? Name each change, or say deed:Nothing. This is what makes the act read-only or not on every surface: an agent will be told it is safe to call, a browser will be allowed to retry it. Is that true?

Who may perform this act? Name a role, not a person, an application or a surface. If the honest answer is 'anyone who can reach it', that is a role too, and worth naming so that it can be withdrawn later.
This act and https://example.org/x#TakeLease have the same resource and the same verb. Are they one act with a parameter, or is one of them about a resource that has not been named?

This act says it reads nothing and also names a state it reads. Which is it?

This act changes https://example.org/x#LeaseState but declares no failure of its own. What happens when https://example.org/x#LeaseState is not as the actor expects: already there, already held, moved on since they looked?
A required yes-or-no has only one useful value. What is the actor confirming? If it is that they have seen the current state, ask for that state instead.
'force' is also the name of https://example.org/x#path. A name means one thing across the tool. Are these the same parameter, or does one of them need a more exact name?
An environment variable is upper case with underscores, and only a setting has one: the environment supplies context, never input. If a parameter seems to want one, is it context?
